claims.text: Introducing dual heterogeneous structures into eutectic high-entropy alloys improves both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
The initial material consists of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The initial lamellar colonies contain numerous internal boundaries.
The structure produced by the intervention is a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The dual-phase microstructure contains a soft FCC phase and a hard BCC/B2 phase.
The soft FCC phase provides tensile ductility.
The hard BCC/B2 phase provides strength.
The dual-phase microstructure hinders grain-boundary sliding during high-temperature deformation.
The dual-phase microstructure hinders dislocation movement during high-temperature deformation.
Hindering grain-boundary sliding and dislocation movement improves high-temperature strength and ductility.
Yield strength may increase by 20–30% relative to the baseline.
Tensile strength may increase by 20–30% relative to the baseline.
Tensile ductility may increase by 10–20% relative to the baseline.
The intervention must maintain the stability of a high-temperature precipitate phase.
Formation of brittle phases must be avoided for the intervention to remain effective.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility improvements depends on alloy composition and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator is described essentially as the initial dual-phase lamellar structure, so the fields do not clearly identify what new dual heterogeneity the intervention creates. The cited intervention instead produced retained lamellar and transformed nanocrystalline regions with structure-composition heterogeneity.

The hypothesis is framed for room-temperature tensile deformation, but part of the proposed mechanism concerns grain-boundary sliding, dislocation motion, and properties during high-temperature deformation.
